strengths: R2E offers a coherent, NLP-relevant approach to evidence-attributed prediction. Entity-specific retrieval, masked answers, and a set transformer trained with missing evidence provide a well-defined basis for passage-level Shapley attribution.

The experiments support the central contribution: adding inspectable evidence while retaining predictive performance. Gene-description MRR reaches 0.260, versus 0.176 for the strongest baseline, and remains competitive without correction at 0.202. Literature-only clinical AUROC essentially matches the MLM baseline: 0.632 versus 0.630.

The literature evaluations include meaningful safeguards: document-level splits, temporal cutoffs, and training encoders from scratch. Retrieval updates, architectural ablations, genetics-only comparisons, and analyses restricted to diseases with genetic insight strengthen the empirical case.

The three public evaluation datasets are useful contributions. Detailed architecture descriptions, hyperparameters, attribution pseudocode, prompts, computational profiling, and candid failure examples support reimplementation and understanding. The supported contribution warrants Findings.
weaknesses: The clinical benchmark supports a narrower interpretation than predicting therapeutic efficacy or discovering novel targets. Appendix P labels discontinued Phase II/III programs as failures despite acknowledging commercial and pharmacological causes. Filtering drugs by earliest development date also does not establish that their target–disease relationships were previously unknown. Results separated by prior target–disease knowledge would better substantiate the discovery claims.

Temporal protection is incomplete for the augmented variants. The genetics evidence comes from Minikel et al. 2024 without a reported pre-2005 restriction, and GPT-4 auditing introduces knowledge with an uncontrolled cutoff. These results require qualification as retrospective analyses using potentially later information. This concern does not invalidate the literature-only result or the comparison using identical genetics data.

Explanation validation remains limited. Shapley values explain scores conditional on the retrieved set and learned NULL intervention. Evidence for scientific relevance relies chiefly on GPT-4 annotations, with clinical AUROC of 0.665; human validation covers only eight hypotheses and one expert. Multiple annotators, agreement adjusted for label prevalence, attribution stability checks, and direct expert evaluation would strengthen the proposed decision-support benefits.

Baseline controls leave some performance attribution unresolved. Frequency correction substantially improves R2E, but the paper omits corrected MLM results even though Appendix G describes how to obtain them. The GPT-4 comparison reports three confidence thresholds rather than an AUROC over all response categories. These omissions weaken conclusions about comparative superiority.

Exact reproducibility is constrained by the proprietary entity linker and training corpus, including licensed full texts, and by explicitly withholding code and model weights. The detailed specification and released evaluation sets are valuable, but an executable reference implementation with results on an accessible corpus would substantially improve reproducibility.

Appendix F contains a localized theoretical inconsistency: Section 3.4 excludes the positive entity when sampling negatives, whereas the derivation assumes independent uniform negatives. Writing p=P(a|q,L=1), the specified sampling gives the optimal logit log((N-1)p/(1-p)), rather than log(Np). Uncorrected ranking remains monotonic in p, but the exact PMI interpretation of the correction in Appendix G needs revision.
